At the clock repair shop, the clocks did not agree. One said ten past four, one said twenty to seven, and a little brass clock shaped like a carriage had been insisting on midnight since March. Customers often pointed this out.

“Yes,” said Mr. Vale. “Imagine the noise otherwise.”

I worked there the summer I was seventeen. My official duties were polishing glass, answering the telephone, and taking down the names of people who called a pendulum “the dangly bit.” My unofficial duty was to climb the ladder whenever Mr. Vale wanted something from a high shelf. He could climb perfectly well. He just felt that youth ought to have some practical application.

One Thursday a woman brought in a kitchen clock the color of a boiled sweet. It had a crack across the number eight and a smear of white paint on its rim.

“It loses eleven minutes a day,” she said.

“When did that start?” I asked, pencil poised.

“Nineteen eighty-six.”

I looked up.

“My husband used to set it every morning,” she explained. “Now I do it, and I’d rather not.”

Mr. Vale took the clock to his bench. The woman had hardly gone before he opened the back and showed me a small plastic movement of the sort that cost less to replace than to repair.

“Five minutes,” I said, pleased with my diagnosis.

“Probably.”

But he spent the afternoon cleaning the case. With a wooden pick he worked the grime from the little channel around the glass. He polished the minute hand. He left the paint alone.

“How did you know she wanted that left on?”

“I didn’t. Easier to take it off later than put it back.”

The woman returned on Saturday. Mr. Vale fitted a battery and let her watch the second hand make a circuit. She paid him, tucked the clock under her arm, and went out. Through the window we saw her stop beside the bus shelter. She took the clock out again. For a moment she held it to her ear, an absurd gesture on a road full of diesel engines. Then the bus came and she got on.

“Do you suppose she wanted it to lose the eleven minutes?” I asked.

“She asked for it fixed.”

“Yes, but do you suppose?”

Mr. Vale handed me the polish. “I suppose that window’s filthy.”

For years afterward I told this story as evidence of his profound understanding of grief. Then I got older and began to suspect he had simply wanted the window cleaned. It was a west-facing window above a busy road. By four in the afternoon every fingerprint shone like the print on a police record.

Last month my daughter brought me a lamp from her first apartment. The switch had gone bad. While I was replacing it, I noticed that someone had written a telephone number in blue ink on the underside of the base. Seven digits, no area code. Beside it was a name I couldn’t quite make out: Dot, perhaps, or Pat.

I had a cloth in my hand. A little alcohol would probably have fetched the ink right off.

“Do you want this number?” I called.

“What number?”

I showed her.

“Oh,” she said. “No idea. It was there when I bought it.”

“Shall I clean it off?”

She considered it. “Does it cost extra to leave it?”

“Considerably.”

“Then put it on my account.”

She took the lamp home. That evening she sent me a photograph of it lit beside her bed. Its shade threw a warm, lopsided circle on the wall. In the circle I could see the pale rectangle where the previous tenant had hung a picture, or a mirror, or possibly a better lamp.

I nearly pointed it out. Instead I enlarged the photograph. On the bedside table were three hairpins, a library book, a glass of water, and the spare key she had been certain she’d left at my house.

I sent the photograph back with the key circled.

A minute later my phone rang.

“Well,” she said, laughing, “that saves me a trip.”

I stood in my kitchen with the cloth still in my hand, listening to her tell me about her day.
